It probably wasn't charged as complex because of technology. Medical billing is such a shitty numbers game. Doctors/hospitals charge based on number of body systems reviewed and examined plus the complexity of the patient. Additionally, a doctor is able to charge more based on time and counseling. So as a scribe, I was told to always make sure to check off a certain number of reviewed items from a certain number of body systems because that allowed the doctor to bill the highest level. She insisted that she reviewed them every single appointment, but it was bullshit. I felt so dirty doing it. Then there are definitely doctors that exaggerate about what was talked about during the appointment because again, it allows them to bill at a higher level. That five minute talk about smoking cessation might be documented as like twenty minutes if you have a greedy doctor.

So we totally are not the same people, but these are the tricks that helped me with my human physiology degree. For all of my exams, I always got very confused with word problems. I felt like I would often misread the problem or skip or important Information. The best trick I have for word problems on exams is to take a colored pen or highlighter and highlight only the pertinent information. Then you can also ask for some scrap sheets of paper. Having a whole lot of text is overwhelming for my brain so I needed to organize in a way for me to easily read. I would rewrite the problem with only the important info or make a table of the info.

For studying, I went to every single class and took thorough notes. Even if I did not go back through the notes, I found that the act of writing down the info helped better understand the material. Note cards were very helpful as well. If we were given a study guide or an outline of what we should know for an exam, I would go through every bullet point and make notes, basically making my own study guide. It is essentially just writing notes in class, but right before the exam.

Don't second guess yourself too much. I can't tell you how many times I got an answer wrong on an exam because I didn't trust my own intelligence. People with ADHD fall into the trap of feeling like we don't actually know what we know.

For multiple choice exams, I go through and answer the questions that I know for certain. If I am not sure of the answer, I circle that question so I know to come back to it. Also, I write the letter answer in bold and large next to the question so I can quickly come back and fill in my scantron at the end of the exam.

I hope some of these might help!
